headline: Thylacine's skull points to a biting style with no match among living mammals
dek: A study in Nature Communications reports that the extinct Tasmanian tiger carried an oversized skull on a small body, built for a fast snapping bite on small prey rather than for taking livestock.
summary: A Nature Communications study reports the extinct thylacine had an unusually large skull and a long, narrow snout suited to a fast snapping bite on small prey, a combination not seen in any living mammal predator.

queries: natural history museum skeleton display glass case
image.alt: Animal skeletons and skulls arranged in glass display cases in a natural history museum gallery.

body.text: The thylacine, the striped marsupial predator of Tasmania and mainland Australia that was declared extinct in the twentieth century, had a skull shaped unlike that of any predator alive today, according to a study published on 31 August 2026 in *Nature Communications*. Flinders University, which announced the work, gives the paper as Weisbecker and colleagues, *Skull morphology of the extinct Tasmanian tiger suggests unique biting style*, DOI 10.1038/s41467-026-76614-0.

The researchers, from Flinders University and the University of Melbourne, compared the shape of thylacine skulls against those of other carnivorous mammals. Sci.News, reporting on the paper, said the comparison ran to specimens from 60 carnivorous mammal species, including wolves, foxes, large cats and extinct marsupial predators. The Flinders announcement does not give a number, and lists the comparison group only as wolves, jackals, foxes and other carnivorous mammals.
A large skull on a small animal

The central observation is a mismatch between the animal's body and its head. Flinders University's announcement puts it in relative terms: an average thylacine weighed roughly half as much as an average wolf, yet its skull was about the size of a grey wolf's.
Even though the average thylacine may have weighed only half as much as the average wolf, its vastly oversized skull is about as large as a grey wolf's skull.
body.cite: Dr Douglass Rovinsky, co-author, via the Flinders University announcement on EurekAlert

body.text: Sci.News gives the body mass as about 17 kilograms and reports that the skull is comparable to those of predators two to four times heavier. It also describes two features of the snout: a widened tip near the canine teeth, and an unusually large opening in the bone below the eye socket, the infraorbital foramen. The Flinders announcement does not carry the 17-kilogram figure, so the two accounts state the animal's size in different ways and we have not reconciled them.

Taken together, the researchers read those traits as an adaptation for a fast, high-impact snapping bite aimed at relatively small and agile prey — animals such as bandicoots — rather than the sustained grip a large predator uses on large prey. The Flinders announcement notes that the closest parallels for that arrangement are found not in mammals at all, but in crocodiles and in predatory fish.

The finding bears on the reason the animal was hunted. Thylacines were pursued under a bounty in Tasmania on the understanding that they preyed on sheep. ABC News reported that a 2011 study had already found the thylacine's jaws too weak to make killing sheep likely, and that the new work is consistent with it: a snapping bite tuned to small, fast prey is not the equipment of a livestock predator.

The paper's lead author has made that connection explicitly. Sci.News quoted Professor Vera Weisbecker of Flinders University saying that the latest findings on the animal's feeding adaptations counter the myths that drove it to extinction. Speaking to ABC News, she framed the loss in broader terms.
When the thylacine was sent extinct, we lost an animal that really was unique to the entire planet.
body.cite: Professor Vera Weisbecker, Flinders University, via ABC News

body.text: She also told ABC News that the thylacine is often thought of as a dog-like animal but is a marsupial, and is reasonably closely related to the Tasmanian devil. The resemblance to a wolf is a matter of convergent shape rather than of kinship, which is part of why comparisons with the dog family have persisted.
What the study does not show

This is an analysis of bone shape, not a record of an animal feeding. No thylacine has been observed hunting in the wild by a researcher with modern equipment, and the inference from skull morphology to diet runs through comparison with living animals whose feeding behaviour is known. Neither the Flinders announcement nor the coverage we read sets out the limitations the authors themselves state in the paper, and we have not read the paper itself.

The number of thylacine skulls examined is also not given in the announcement or in the reporting we opened. Museum collections hold a limited number of specimens, and how many were available to this analysis is a fair question to put to the paper rather than to the coverage of it.

body.title: The animal
items: Thylacinus cynocephalus, a marsupial carnivore once found across Australia and New Guinea and, in historical times, in Tasmania.
It is a marsupial, more closely related to the Tasmanian devil than to any dog, despite the wolf-like outline.
The last known captive animal died in 1936; the species was later declared extinct.

uncertain: The number of thylacine skulls examined. Neither the Flinders University announcement nor the coverage we read states it.

The animal's body mass. Sci.News gives about 17 kilograms; the Flinders announcement gives only a relative figure, roughly half the mass of an average wolf. The two are not obviously in conflict but we could not reconcile them from the sources we opened.
The number of comparison species. Sci.News reports 60 carnivorous mammal species; the Flinders announcement gives no number.
The limitations the authors state in the paper. We read the announcement and the coverage, not the paper, and none of them sets out what the authors say the analysis cannot show.
Dr Douglass Rovinsky's institutional affiliation. Sci.News places him at the Australian Museum; the Flinders announcement names him without an affiliation.
Whether other researchers accept the conclusion that the thylacine's skull has no functional match among living mammals. We found no comment from a researcher outside the study team.
How far the finding settles the historical question of thylacine predation on sheep. The study is about what the skull was suited to, not a record of what individual animals did.
